On November 18, 2026, Cloudflare made two of its AI models free to download. Called Clairic and Clairic-flash, they pull data out of documents such as invoices and receipts. A company can now run these models locally , on its own servers, without sending its documents to an online service.

Both models read a block of text, a photo or a PDF page. They pick out specific pieces of information, such as a supplier’s name, a total amount or a date.

Cloudflare is the US company best known for the network that protects and speeds up websites. It released both models under Apache 2.0, an open-source license that allows commercial use and modification. The release covers the models’ weights. These are the billions of numbers, called parameters, that a model learns during training.

Clairic has 27 billion parameters and Clairic-flash has 9 billion. Cloudflare still sells both as a paid service on Workers AI, its platform for running AI models on its own network.

## Two models that fill in fields

Both models work by filling in a form. They receive a document and a list of fields, and each field has a set type: text, number, date, duration, list, estimate or forecast. For each field, they return one value plus a confidence score that says how sure the model is. When the value appears word for word in the document, they also give its exact position.

Cloudflare files these models under a category it calls “System One,” named after the fast mode of thinking described by psychologist Daniel Kahneman. Cloudflare credits the idea to TypeSafe, a company whose Jev model was built for one specific job and priced low.

Cloudflare says its models of this kind usually answer in under a second. By its account, a large language model, the general-purpose kind of AI behind chatbots, takes several seconds to reason through the same step.

## One month after the preview

Cloudflare first showed Clairic on October 19, 2026, as a preview: a test version available only as an online service. The announcement said Cloudflare intended to release the weights “soon.”

The October post also explained the name: Clairic partly comes from “clair,” the French word for “clear,” as in “Clair de lune.” Cloudflare said the model is meant to extract data clearly and keep the books accurate.

The versions released on November 18 can read PDFs, which the preview could not. They accept up to four images or PDF pages per request. They can also return the line items of an invoice as rows that keep each description, quantity and price together.

Clairic follows Clef and Clef-flash, two models Cloudflare released under the same license on October 1. These are “decision” models, which sort a piece of content into one of several options and give a probability for each.

The November 18 post is signed by Alex Reneau, Michelle Chen and Kevin Flansburg. In it, Cloudflare says it has become a “neolab,” meaning a lab that builds its own cutting-edge AI models. The team calls itself the Workers AI “superintelligence team.”

## The scores Cloudflare reports

Cloudflare published four internal evaluations. The first covered 336 text fields drawn from 96 requests. Clairic extracted 335 of them correctly, Clairic-flash 328 and the October preview 295.

The second test used 576 fields from made-up receipts, shown as text and as images. Both new models got all 576 right, while the preview made 207 errors. In the third test, on 226 fields from mixed inputs, Clairic got 221 right and Clairic-flash 213.

The November 18 post also compares the Clairic models with two rivals. One is D1.2, from the company Liquid AI, run together with Apple’s text recognition tool. The other is Extract, from a company called Scaledown. On the 576 receipt fields, D1.2 got 397 right and Extract 280.

The fourth test used 1,263 checks drawn from customer cases that Cloudflare tracks. Both Clairic models passed all 1,263. D1.2 passed 973 and Extract 653.

Cloudflare also measured how fast each model returns a complete answer on a server it runs itself. On text fields, Clairic-flash returned half its answers in under 155 milliseconds, or thousandths of a second, and 95% in under 328. Clairic, nearly three times larger, was slower: 358 milliseconds for half its answers and 736 for 95%.

## Built on Alibaba’s Qwen, and demanding to set up

The blog post does not say what the models are built on. Their pages on Hugging Face, a site for sharing AI models, do: Clairic is built on Qwen3.8-27B and Clairic-flash on Qwen3.5-9B. Both base models come from Qwen, a family of open models made by China’s Alibaba. Cloudflare gave them extra training for data extraction and added components that output numbers, dates, estimates and calculations.

The files are large. Clairic’s weights take up about 56 gigabytes and Clairic-flash’s about 20. Each model’s download also holds 72 files of code in Python, a programming language. They include modules for receipt totals, tables and the lines of a document that hold numbers.

The model page asks for Python 3.11 or later, and its code loads the model onto an Nvidia graphics card. Several of the libraries it lists for faster math can be installed only on Linux machines with Intel or AMD x86 processors.

Cloudflare has not released the models in GGUF, the file format used by Ollama, llama.cpp and LM Studio, common tools for running AI on a personal computer. The blog post, model pages and documentation do not list the supported languages.

## Pricing and terms on Workers AI

On Workers AI, Cloudflare bills only for the tokens the model reads, meaning the small units of text sent to it. The tokens it writes in reply are free.

Until December 1, both models cost $0.10 per million tokens read. After that, Clairic’s price rises to $0.24, while Clairic-flash stays at $0.10.

According to the documentation, the models reread the document for each text field requested. Each reread bills the whole document and its images again. A request with ten text fields is therefore billed, in principle, for ten reads. Fields are grouped together only when a document is too long for the model’s working memory, the amount of text it can handle at once.

The Workers AI documentation says the data customers send is not kept (“zero data retention”). It still labels both models as previews, although the blog post says Clairic is out of preview.

During the preview, Clairic’s address on Workers AI served a 9-billion-parameter model. That model is moving to a separate address under the name Clairic-flash. Apps still connected to the old address will get the new 27-billion-parameter Clairic automatically as the rollout proceeds.

## In-house tests and a reworked design

Cloudflare itself acknowledges the limits of its numbers. It writes that there is no public benchmark for extraction yet, meaning no standard test that anyone can run to compare models. It asks readers to treat its internal evaluations as a rough guide. On November 18, Unite.AI, a trade site that covers AI, noted that these results do not allow an independent ranking of extraction models.

The new Clairic also works differently from the preview. In October, Cloudflare said the preview produced each answer in a single computation instead of writing it out one token at a time. On that basis, it argued the preview could not “hallucinate,” meaning invent an answer the way a large language model does. Cloudflare added that the preview could still make mistakes.

The new Clairic, by contrast, writes its answers one token at a time for ordinary text and number fields. The November 18 post admits that it “technically” produces output tokens, which Cloudflare chooses not to bill.

In October, Cloudflare also listed the preview’s weak spots: multistep calculations, the reliability of its error margins, and its forecasts, which it called “basic.” At the time, it advised leaving the math to ordinary code. The new Clairic adds components trained for arithmetic and date calculations. The November 18 post gives no results specific to those calculations.

## What it means

The release matters most to companies that do not want to send their invoices, contracts or expense reports to an online service. Both models can now run on a company’s own hardware. Their license also carries none of the limits that French AI company Mistral added for resellers with its Large 4 model .

Similar products launched this fall remain hosted services that apps call over the internet. They include OpenAI’s Decisions API and the document-reading API that Chinese AI company DeepSeek has sold since November 13 .

Installation is still demanding. The model page calls for an Nvidia graphics card, a Linux server and room for 20 to 56 gigabytes of weights, with no compressed version released. Ollama and LM Studio users cannot yet launch these models in a few clicks.

Every accuracy figure comes from Cloudflare’s own test sets. Several things remain unknown: how well the two models handle non-English documents, how they perform on real company invoices in tests run outside Cloudflare, and the minimum recommended hardware.

Two signs will show whether the models catch on outside Cloudflare. The first would be a compressed or GGUF version, released by Cloudflare or by outside developers. After Clef came out, Cloudflare says, it saw many experiments and retrained versions. The second would be a first independent test on real documents.

The December 1 price change will show whether Workers AI customers pay $0.24 per million tokens for Clairic or switch to Clairic-flash at $0.10.

The Italian company Domyn has run training trials for EUROPA, the European Union’s open AI model, on a public supercomputer. The test setup has nearly 1 trillion parameters, more than double the minimum the European Commission set. Domyn, which the Commission picked in June to build EUROPA, described the trials in a technical post on November 12, 2026.

Parameters are the internal settings a model learns during training. In its test setup, EUROPA has 951.9 billion of them. The supercomputer, JUPITER, is in Jülich, Germany, and is shared with hundreds of other projects. Domyn says it made training on the machine 14 times faster than at the start of its tests.

Domyn has not yet released EUROPA’s weights, the files that hold its parameters and let anyone run it on their own hardware . It plans to publish them with details of its training methods when EUROPA comes out. The post gives no date. In June, the outlet Declic Media reported that Domyn was aiming for a release “within the year.”

## A project the Commission picked in June

On February 13, 2026, the European Commission launched the Frontier AI Grand Challenge. It ran the contest with the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking, which oversees Europe’s network of public supercomputers. The goal was to pick one project to train a frontier model, a top-tier AI system, with at least 400 billion parameters. The winner gets up to 2.5% of EuroHPC’s total computing capacity for one year.

On June 19, the Commission named the winner: the EUROPA consortium. Domyn, a Milan company formerly known as iGenius, leads the group. Its partners are two German institutes from the Fraunhofer research network, IAIS and IIS. The Commission wants open models that public authorities, researchers and businesses can use. EUROPA also has to cover all 24 official EU languages.

“Europe can lead in advanced AI on its own terms,” said Henna Virkkunen, the Commission’s executive vice president for tech sovereignty, security and democracy.

## How the 951.9 billion parameters are organized

Domyn says it aimed for about 1 trillion parameters, the size of today’s frontier models. The Commission’s minimum was 400 billion.

EUROPA uses a design called “mixture of experts.” The network is split into 384 specialized sub-networks, called experts. A model reads text in small units called tokens, each roughly a word or part of a word. Only 8 of the 384 experts work on any given token. As a result, only 32.8 billion of the 951.9 billion parameters are active for each token. That cuts the amount of computing needed.

During training, the model reads text in sequences of 65,536 tokens. Domyn notes that these figures come from its trials and that “some values may change before the training run starts.”

## JUPITER, a shared machine built for science

According to the Jülich research center, JUPITER is Europe’s first exascale supercomputer. That means it can perform more than a quintillion (a billion billion) operations per second. The EuroHPC Joint Undertaking owns the machine and is putting €250 million into it. The German federal government and the state of North Rhine-Westphalia are each contributing €125 million.

Domyn uses JUPITER’s Booster module, a section of the machine with 5,884 nodes, the networked computers that make up the machine. Each node has four NVIDIA GH200 chips. Each chip pairs a general-purpose processor, or CPU, with a GPU, the processor that does most of the AI math.

According to Domyn, models this size have mostly been trained on dedicated clusters of NVIDIA’s newer Blackwell chips. On JUPITER, Domyn has only user-level access. That means it cannot change the operating system, the network or the nodes’ memory, all of which are set up for scientific simulation.

The network between nodes is the bottleneck. Training can run several copies of the model in parallel, and each copy spans 384 GPUs across 96 nodes. Those nodes have to exchange data. But the link between two nodes is 36 times slower than the link between a GPU and the CPU on its own chip.

## From 90 to about 1,300 tokens per second per GPU

At first, each GPU processed 90 tokens per second and spent most of its time waiting for data from the network. Domyn started by making the text sequences longer, giving the GPUs more work between exchanges. The team then moved some intermediate data, the temporary results of the calculations, to the CPU’s memory to free up memory on the GPU.

Domyn also moved the heaviest part of the optimizer, an algorithm called Muon, from the CPU to the GPU. The optimizer adjusts the parameters at each training step, one round of learning. Its work on each step dropped from 41.7 seconds to 2.2 seconds.

Other changes cut the amount of data sent over the network. The experts’ weights, the values of their parameters, now travel compressed in FP8 format, at 8 bits per value. The gradients, the corrections computed at each step, travel in bf16 format, at 16 bits per value.

A fix to memory management raised throughput, the number of tokens processed per second, by 21%. In the end, each GPU processed 1,293 tokens per second, up from 90 at the start. Domyn contributed its fixes back to PyTorch and TorchTitan, the open-source software it uses to train the model.

At that rate, one copy of the model processes about 43 billion tokens a day, according to Domyn. With four copies running in parallel on 1,536 GPUs, the company puts the total at about 150 billion tokens a day. At that scale, each GPU keeps 89% of the speed it reaches when a single copy runs.

The Italian daily Quotidiano Nazionale concludes that full pretraining, the main phase of learning from raw text, would take about four months.

## What the trials do not show yet

The post opens by saying the company has “recently started training” a frontier-scale model. Yet the rest of the text describes only trials. The throughput figures are median values, measured over steps 4 through 10 of each trial. The setup may also change before the training run starts.

Quotidiano Nazionale put it this way: the demonstration “does not yet amount to completing the training.”

Domyn also flags its own uncertainties. A rule that spreads tokens evenly across four groups of 96 experts, one group per GPU, speeds up the computing. But Domyn says that, based on its early runs, this rule “can indeed hurt training.”

The company says FP8 compression and bf16 gradients do not measurably change the model’s loss, the gap between its predictions and the actual text. Its comparisons, however, cover only ten training steps. The post says nothing about the training data, the share of each language, expected performance or the license.

## Domyn Edge and Europe’s other projects

Domyn has already released a much smaller open model, Domyn Edge, which it began rolling out on October 20, 2026. It has 4 billion parameters, compared with 951.9 billion for EUROPA’s test setup. Domyn trained it from scratch on 13 trillion tokens. It used Leonardo, a European supercomputer hosted by the CINECA computing center in Italy.

Domyn Edge is released under the Apache 2.0 license, an open-source license that allows commercial use. The release also includes part of the training data, the code and intermediate versions of the model. French is one of its five main languages.

In June, Declic Media reported that Europe was running at least three large “sovereign” AI model projects in parallel, meaning models developed under European control. One of them, OpenEuroLLM, has a budget of €37.4 million and announced models of 7 billion to 175 billion parameters. Declic Media added that EUROPA’s target went beyond anything Europe had attempted so far. Its author also noted that Domyn’s model “hasn’t written its first line of weights.”

## What it means

The November 12 post shows a project much larger than the Commission asked for. The Commission required at least 400 billion parameters, and the consortium is aiming for about 1 trillion. Domyn’s test measurements suggest that a shared public machine built for science can train a model this size at a workable speed. So far, though, this is an engineering demonstration. The full training run still has to happen, and then the model has to be evaluated and released.

In the private sector, the French company Mistral AI released the weights of Mistral Large 4 , a model with about 1 trillion parameters, on October 29. Mistral is backed by private investors and says it trained the model in its own data centers in Europe.

Running EUROPA on in-house hardware would take a lot of memory, even with the usual compression to 4 bits per parameter. At that level, its weights alone would take up at least 476 GB by our math, plus working memory. That puts it in the same range as Muse Spark Open, Meta’s open model . That model has 816 billion parameters and runs on two Apple Mac Studio desktops with 512 GB of memory each.

Several questions remain open. Neither the Commission nor Domyn has named EUROPA’s license, the legal terms for using it. The training data, the share of French in it, the model’s benchmark test scores and the release date are all still unknown.

EuroHPC’s grant of computing time lasts only one year. Three milestones are worth watching: the actual start of the full training run, the reports Domyn plans to publish “as the training run progresses,” and the technical report on Domyn Edge, expected in November.
